World.title: Georgian prosecutors question another Formula employee. What’s happening at TV channel?
World.content:
The case against Georgia’s Formula TV

Georgia‘s Prosecutor’s Office has summoned Formula cameraman Misho Martashvili for questioning as part of an investigation into the television channel. He is due to appear before investigators today. Journalist Nata Lomadze and TV presenter Davit Kashiashvili have already been questioned in connection with the same case.

Kashiashvili said he hoped prosecutors would drop the investigation.

“I can’t imagine what purpose would be served by continuing this case, although the public can judge for itself. They have already questioned me, the author of the report, and now cameraman Misho Martashvili. I hope the Prosecutor’s Office will soon announce that it is ending the criminal investigation.”

What’s happening at Formula?

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, a criminal investigation has been opened under a provision of Georgia’s Criminal Code covering the filing of a knowingly false accusation. Prosecutors say the case was launched following a complaint by lawyers representing film director Goga Khaindrava.

The investigation relates to a Formula report based on an anonymous source. The report alleged that, in 2016 and 2017, Khaindrava helped arrange the entry of Indian and Pakistani nationals into Georgia in exchange for payment, in coordination with the State Security Service.

Khaindrava and the Prosecutor’s Office argue that the report may have involved the unlawful interception of communications, prompting the criminal investigation.

Alongside the criminal case, Khaindrava has also filed a civil lawsuit against Formula. He alleges that the broadcaster published false and defamatory claims about him and is seeking compensation for non-material damage to his honour and reputation.

Formula’s lawyer says the civil claim does not meet the legal threshold required for it to succeed.

The case against Georgia’s Formula TV

World.title: Abkhaz diaspora in Turkey calls for recognition of Abkhazia’s independence – or at least Abkhaz passports
World.content:
A campaign urging the Turkish government to review its policy towards Abkhazia is gathering momentum in Turkey. Organised by the local Abkhaz diaspora, it calls on Ankara to recognise Abkhaz identity documents and establish direct sea and air links with Abkhazia.

Most countries, including Turkey, support UN and European Union resolutions that describe Abkhazia as part of Georgia’s territory under Russian occupation. Russia recognised Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states after the August 2008 war with Georgia over South Ossetia, also known as the Tskhinvali region. Besides Russia, the independence of the two regions is currently recognised only by Nicaragua, Venezuela, Nauru and Syria.

An estimated 500,000 ethnic Abkhazians live in Turkey. Representatives of the community are urging Turkish citizens to submit petitions through the Turkish Presidency’s Communication Centre, calling on the government to recognise the Republic of Abkhazia.

As an initial step, they are asking Ankara to recognise Abkhaz passports as valid travel and identity documents, and to establish direct sea and air links between Turkey and Abkhazia.

According to the organisers, the campaign aims to draw attention to what they describe as the humanitarian consequences of Abkhazia’s isolation, arguing that it restricts residents’ rights to freedom of movement, education, healthcare and maintaining family ties.

The organisers say the campaign is open not only to members of Caucasian communities in Turkey, but to all Turkish citizens who support the protection of human rights.

In an explanatory note, the organisers point to existing international precedents, citing Taiwan as an example.

“Despite the ‘One China’ policy, relations with Taiwan are maintained through de facto representative offices. Air services operate on the basis of technical arrangements and commercial agreements between Turkey’s Directorate General of Civil Aviation and Taiwan’s aviation authorities, without the need for formal intergovernmental treaties,” the document says.

Addressing the International Civil Aviation Organization’s restrictions on flights to Abkhazia, the campaign’s organisers argue that Turkey could instead follow the model used for flights to the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which, like Abkhazia, has only limited international recognition.

On 4 July, the initiative received backing from Turkey’s Labour Party, which published a statement on its official platforms calling for an end to Abkhazia’s isolation and endorsing the diaspora’s demands.

World.title: Grandmother's 32-hour bus 'adventure' home after train shutdown
World.content:
Rita Busbridge had travelled from Victoria's surf coast to Sydney to watch her grandson perform with his school at the iconic Sydney Opera House.

But what should have been a trip remembered for a treasured family moment turned into what felt like an intrepid adventure.

The 78-year-old from Torquay had booked a 7am train trip home on Wednesday with her daughter-in-law, who wanted to have an "experience" on the interstate rail network.

They only got as far as Campbelltown, an hour south-west of Sydney, when the trains ground to a halt.

Wednesday's nationwide Telstra outage paused regional trains in NSW and Victoria, with the southern state's V/Line network shut down completely for over 24 hours.

Passengers wait for replacement buses at Southern Cross station. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The pair waited with other passengers for a replacement bus, which returned them to Sydney Central.

After waiting at a bus terminal there all day, she managed to catch a 9pm coach to Melbourne, while her daughter-in-law stayed in Sydney.

Ms Busbridge managed a few hours sleep during the drive, but the bus broke down at Broadford in central Victoria at 7am, about an hour from Southern Cross station in Melbourne's CBD.

"We were stuck there for another hour and a half, two hours, then another bus came and replaced that," Ms Busbridge said.

"We went to Southern Cross, I was able to get a coffee, a pit stop, then back on the bus to come down to Marshall [in Geelong]."

She then walked 20 minutes to her car, and drove home to Torquay, with the entire trip taking over 32 hours instead of the planned 13.

"I think we need to be aware that we can't always rely on technology. We need to be self-sufficient," she said.

Despite the chaotic journey home, Rita viewed the trip as an "adventure".

"[My daughter-in-law and I] often say we're going on an adventure, but she decided to pull out of the adventure," she said wryly.

"One of my other sons always says 'slow and steady wins the race', so that's I think another really good bit of advice."

More bus pain for Victorian travellers

After two days of confusion and uncertainty during the shutdown, regional commuters are enduring more bus replacement services today, with planned works taking place.

There is also no clear timeline for when passengers will receive compensation from V/Line for out-of-pocket expenses caused by the cancellations.

Buses are replacing trains on the busy Bendigo, Ballarat and Geelong lines due to planned works from 10pm Friday night until the last service on Saturday night, as well as on the Warrnambool, Ararat, Maryborough and Swan Hill lines.

There will also be bus replacement services on the Williamstown, Werribee and Sunbury metro lines.

Buses will continue to replace trains in the evenings on some regional lines into next week.

V/Line has warned passengers to prepare for a busy Saturday at Southern Cross Station.

"The replacement coach terminal at Southern Cross Station will be extremely busy on Saturday 11 July," it said.

"Please allow extra time for your journey, follow directional signage and listen for announcements."

Victoria's regional rail network was hit particularly hard by the outage, causing trains to lose communications.

Trains resumed on Thursday afternoon, but for many a weekend of buses awaits. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Replacement buses were brought in but could not meet passenger demands, leading to many travellers forking out to stay in hotels or for expensive taxi and rideshare trips.

Leanne Butler travelled from Kyneton to Melbourne on Wednesday for a day in the city with her 10 and 11-year-old sons and her sister.

While the trip down on the bus went smoothly, their trip home did not.

"We set off and our first stop was Clarkfield, [and] on the way the bus kept making a beeping," she said .

Ms Butler said the driver couldn't get the bus into gear and kept reversing on a busy road, stalled on a roundabout then came to a stop near a service station at Bulla.

"We weren't really told much but [the driver] was trying his hardest to get the bus going but couldn't," she said.

No-one was sure if there would be a replacement bus so the family had to find their own way home, which she says was "pretty scary" for her kids.

"People were ringing families, friends to come get them, as well as Ubers," she said.

"Some were still stranded when we left which was around 7.30pmish, maybe.

"I think the whole experience was pretty bad to leave people stranded for god only knows."

Free V/Line services on Monday and Tuesday

Train services did not resume until 12pm on Thursday.

More than 200 buses were used on the first day trains stopped running, while 180 replaced scheduled services on Thursday.

V/Line staff reported that patronage on Friday morning appeared to be typical of a normal day.

The state government said V/Line would reimburse passengers left out of pocket by the Telstra network failure, and transport would be free on the service on Monday and Tuesday.

It has also called on Telstra to match those repayments "dollar for dollar".

"Telstra has to pay a price," senior minister Lily D'Ambrosio said on Friday morning.

She said the government and V/Line were working through the logistics of issuing the compensation, and money had been set aside, but there was currently no time for when that would be available.

Telstra's CEO Vicki Brady on Friday said she was "deeply sorry" for the outage.

World.title: Adrenaline junkie 89yo skydives to celebrate his birthday
World.content:
A Queensland grandfather has celebrated his 89th birthday by skydiving over the Sunshine Coast with his 39-year-old grandson.

Donald Walker says he is "terrified of getting old" and adventure doesn't have an expiry date.

He and his grandson jumped out of a plane 13,000 feet over Noosa and spent a minute freefalling before enjoying a roughly five minute glide down in the parachute before landing on Coolum Beach.

This was Donald's third time skydiving, after his first jump when he was 70, also a birthday celebration.

Donald Walker alongside his grandson before the skydive. (Supplied: Skydive Australia)

He said he had wanted to take to the skies since he was a boy, after he watched C-47 planes tow gliders as they flew over his home during World War II.

But "life got in the way", and he would have to wait years before experiencing the thrill of jumping for himself.

Donald said his favourite part of a dive is the moments just after the free-fall, when the main parachute opens and "everything just stops".

"It's like as though you're not moving, even though you're still falling, and it just feels so peaceful," he said.

"It's quiet, you can hear things, hear birds in the air.

"It's just beautiful."

Donald Walker says he intends to skydive for as long as he can. (Supplied: Skydive Australia)

Donald, who does not consider himself old, said he hoped to continue skydiving until he "gets a letter from the king".

"I intend to do it as long as I can," he said.

"At least once a year, more if I can get it."

He said some people think his hobby is "weird", but Donald believes no one is too old for an adventure.

" If you keep your body and your mind going and turning over, you always feel better. "

Donald was all smiles before the skydive. (Supplied: Skydive Australia)

Donald isn't alone in chasing thrills at an older age, according to SkyDive Australia Chief Commercial Officer Fiona Stillwell.

She says there is an entire generation of older Australians who are taking up the hobby of jumping out of a plane.

Skydive Australia data shows a total of 14,491 people over the age of 50 have chosen to dive since 2023.

More than 269 of those were over the age of 75, the data points out, showing that Donald definitely is part of a strong group of thrill seeking grandparents.

World.title: 'Healing from trauma': The fashion show not about the dresses
World.content:
Esperance Nyirabarahinyuza is pacing around the front room of a weatherboard house-turned-community hub in Woodridge, south of Brisbane.

There are about a dozen women inside, crowded around sewing machines and needles, weaving together vibrant, multi-coloured dresses.

The house the women are in is home to Women's Power of Inspiration (WPI), a not-for-profit organisation Esperance set up to help address loneliness and isolation felt within the refugee and migrant community in Logan.

The rhythmic thuds of the machines cut through the room as the women slowly move the cloth across the benchtop.

"Try this," the 63-year-old tells one of them. "Good job," she says to another.

Esperance helps teach some of the group how to make the vibrant dresses. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)

The African continent, seen on a globe at the front of the room, acts as a reminder of the places many of these women once called home.

A reminder of the atrocities many, including Esperance, have lived through.

"We have trauma, torture, we have lost country and everything," she said.

"But we are in this beautiful country."

The organisation started with a simple barbecue between a handful of women. Now it has grown to over 100 members.

Together, they make dresses, bags and other traditional items.

Esperance set up the group to help address loneliness and isolation felt within the refugee and migrant community in Logan. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)

But while the sewing gives the women a reason to come together, the conversations that follow are what matter most.

Esperance arrived in Australia in 2002 after surviving the Rwandan genocide in the 1990s.

"[My story] is hard to tell, it's heartbreaking," she said.

In 1994, hundreds of thousands of Tutsi and moderate Hutu people were slaughtered over 100 days by Hutu militia. Rape was also used as a weapon.

In the aftermath of the genocide, millions fled the country to refugee camps in neighbouring countries such as the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

One of Esperance's few photographs from her life in Rwanda. (Supplied: Esperance Nyirabarahinyuza)

Esperance, who had been a schoolteacher in Rwanda, and her family, were caught in the crossfire and had to leave.

They spent years in refugee camps in the DRC, Kenya and Uganda.

"For me even to seek food for my kids, it was so hard," she said.

Esperance's husband and two children were killed in an attack on a refugee camp in Uganda, while she was left with severe head injuries.

It was just days before she was due to fly out to Australia.

Family photographs of some of the infants and children who died hang on display in an exhibition at the Kigali Genocide Memorial centre. (AP: Ben Curtis)

"I remember [when I met my] support worker at the airport [in Australia] she was crying, saying 'where are the kids,'" she said.

Esperance said for her and many other migrants coming to Australia from conflict zones, the trauma was not left at the border.

"When I came here, I had one year where I did not open my mouth and speak my Kinyarwanda tongue because there was no Kinyarwanda here.

"I asked my God 'how can I dream in my language' ... I did not dream."

Esperance remarried while living in Melbourne in 2009 and soon after welcomed her son Prynce into the world.

But when Prynce was 18 months old, he had a stroke and was left with severe disabilities, leading Esperance to withdraw from the world again.

Esperance remarried in Melbourne in 2009. (Supplied: Esperance Nyirabarahinyuza)

"For me, it was the end of the life. I've been hiding in the house, hiding him," she said.

In 2022 and now living in Woodridge in Logan, a neighbour approached Esperance.

"My neighbour said to me 'enough is enough, you have to get out … you're not looking after yourself,'" she said.

"I thought 'I don't speak good English, but I have an education'. Why can't I go and then be with other women? I know I'm not alone."

That idea inspired her to start Women's Power of Inspiration in Logan, home to people from more than 200 cultural backgrounds.

Since then, women have come together to learn English, understand Australian finances, recognise domestic violence, prepare for work and, perhaps most importantly, support one another.

Silvia Niyonsaba says the group is a place for healing. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)

Silvia Niyonsaba helped set up the group alongside Esperance, with the idea to help women who brought their trauma into Australia to move forward with their lives.

"We tried to find something that can help women [be calm]," she said.

"WPI, it's a good place. It's a healing place. It has healed many women. Me too."

Godeberthe Gwahekazi has showcased dresses she has made at the group's annual fashion gala and regularly attends gatherings at the home.

"This community is like we are home. It's our family," she said.

"It's our future. Because we help each other in all needs and we can feel like our life keeps moving."

At the end of May, the women gathered at a community centre at Slacks Creek where the dresses they made were paraded down a catwalk.

Members of the Women’s Power of Inspiration group held a fashion show earlier this year. (Supplied)

The annual gala has become a fixture since WPI was founded, but now they are struggling to make the event financially viable.

Esperance said this year's event might be the last for a while.

"It's heartbreaking, because it's good for our women who make the dresses and then walk on stage and do modelling," she said afterwards.

"It's just a lot of effort. We need support.

The annual gala has become a fixture since WPI was founded. (Supplied)

"It's not about the dresses, it's not about that. It's about healing."

Logan City Councillor Teresa Lane, who helped WPI obtain the lease to the council-owned house they are currently based in, said the gala was a highlight for the community and local government was helping the organisation navigate challenges.

"We are going to hunt for some sponsors and see if we can keep it going, maybe even expand it a little bit," she said.

Logan City Councillor Teresa Lane helped Esperance secure the lease for the building the women's group is based. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)

While the showcase might be taking a break for the foreseeable future, Esperance said the women will still be getting together.

Back at the house in Woodridge, laughter drifts from one corner, as a small group share stories in multiple languages.

They are still working. They are still making clothes. And laughing, crying, and supporting each other through their trauma.

The group of women are hoping to find sponsors to keep their fashion show event going. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus)

"A woman who has been in a refugee camp for 40 years, she's born in a camp, she'd never do this," Esperance said.

"But she is here. She is sewing and she goes out and shows the dresses she's made.

"She's saying 'I'm here.'"

World.title: Handmade quilts babies 'will have for life' wrap them in culture
World.content:
On Worimi Country in northern New South Wales, a baby's tiny hand clutches a handmade patchwork quilt, eyes captivated by its striking red, black and yellow patterns.

The quilt is one of many gifted to families during a NAIDOC Week baby celebration at Forster's Tobwabba Aboriginal Medical Service.

The annual event brings together Indigenous mothers and local elders to celebrate babies born over the past year, strengthen community connections and honour each child's cultural heritage.

This year, Jenny Fletcher from the MidCoast Community Quilters group based at Nabiac collaborated with Worimi elders to create about 20 patchwork quilts for the celebration.

Jenny Fletcher says creating Indigenous-themed quilts for the baby blessing was very rewarding. (ABC News: Emma Siossian)

"You feel good … we are proud of what we do," she said.

"You put your heart and soul into it.

"We get a lot of satisfaction, playing with the vibrant colours and the Indigenous [patterned] fabrics."

Donna Hall says the baby blessing was about recognising the next generation. (ABC News: Wiriya Sati)

Worimi elder Aunty Donna Hall said the baby celebration was held annually around NAIDOC Week and the handmade quilts would be a special memento for families.

"The baby shower is a very important thing; it's recognising the next generation," she said.

"The main thing is the connection, not only to the mums and bubs and grandparents, but also to the older siblings.

Tamara Close holds her daughter at the baby celebration at the Tobwabba Aboriginal Medical Service. (ABC News: Wiriya Sati)

"Babies tend to get attached to their little rugs … the quilts make an important thing for those babes as they get older."

NAIDOC Week 2026: 50 Years of Deadly The ABC has gathered the best First Nations films, TV shows and documentaries to enjoy during NAIDOC Week.

One of the mothers at the blessing, Lylah-Belle Wilson said it was a great chance to connect with other Indigenous mums.

Ms Wilson said she was delighted to receive a handmade patchwork for her son Coda.

"It's just really special to receive the blanket on his first NAIDOC … we've just converted his room. It will go on his 'big-boy' bed," she said.

Jenny Fletcher hands one of her handmade quilts to Lylah-Belle Wilson and her son Coda. (ABC News: Wiriya Sati)

"I think it's really special to acknowledge in our situation our culture and history; and also to bring awareness to people who aren't familiar with the week and the celebration.

"It's lovely to see a lot of the other mums: Coda's aunts and cousins."

Another recipient, Crystal Heavey, said her son Bilgarli's handmade quilt would be treasured through the years.

Baby Bilgarli with his new handmade quilt, which his mum Crystal says he "will have for life". (ABC News: Wiriya Sati)

"He's going to have this for the rest of his life, and he'll always know that this is his little NAIDOC blanket," she said.

NAIDOC Week runs until July 12.

It is a celebration of First Nations people, and the theme this year is "50 Years of Deadly".

As part of the baby celebration at Forster, tiny feet were painted in Indigenous colours, pressed onto paper as a memento and themed baby photographs were taken to add to a photo wall, commemorating the region's youngest residents.

The excitement of the foot painting and celebration caught up with young Bilgarli. (ABC News: Wiriya Sati)

Zarlia Murgha said it was great to be there with her daughter.

Find stories of ancient Australia near you There are ways to see into the deep past all around the country.

"I am so connected to culture; I can't wait for her to get into all that as well," she said.

For quilters such as Annette Davis, the occasion is about much more than showing off craft skills.

"I think it's a very lovely way of introducing the Aboriginal children into the community and I am happy to be part of that," she said.

Quilts for comfort

Beyond the NAIDOC baby blessing, the MidCoast Community Quilters make about 600 quilts a year to donate to community groups, including the Great Lakes Women's Shelter.

The shelter's Liahna Paulson, a Worimi woman, said the quilts brought comfort to those rebuilding their lives.

Liahna Paulson holds one of the quilts donated to the Great Lakes Women's Shelter. (ABC News: Emma Siossian)

"The women and children who come into the shelter absolutely love them," she said.

"It gives them that safe and secure feeling, especially coming in from something traumatic, such as domestic violence or homelessness.

The MidCoast Community Quilters have donated more than 5,000 quilts over the past decade. (ABC News: Emma Siossian)

"The kids get very attached to the blankets … so they become their little comforter and when they find a new home they take them with them and have them for a long time."

Ms Fletcher said the MidCoast Community Quilters planned to keep gifting their handmade creations.

Some of the members of the MidCoast Community Quilters, with Worimi elder Aunty Janice Paulson. (ABC News: Emma Siossian)

"When you hear stories of the feedback, it makes you want to sew more; it gives you a warm spot," she said.

"Quilts are like friends. They give warmth and comfort when needed, so that's what we aim to do."

World.title: The 99-year-old Victorian mechanic still working six days a week
World.content:
Locals call it the Mallee Track.

A 185-kilometre section of the Mallee Highway, it stretches from Manangatang in north-west Victoria to the South Australian border.

And near the midpoint on this often-lonely road is a garage.

Its fuel bowsers stand to attention as if saluting the passing traffic.

A car drives by the A.J. Gloster workshop on the Mallee Track at Underbool. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

Welcome to Underbool, a town of just 215 people where an unremarkable steel-clad building holds a rather remarkable tale and a possible world record holder.

Walk into the workshop, and you'll be greeted by the garage's head mechanic, 99-year-old Ray Gloster.

Ray Gloster (right), pictured here with his son Robert Gloster, shows no signs of slowing down. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

Ray has worked at A.J. Gloster and Sons for 83 years.

He still turns up six days a week to work on local vehicles and sometimes the cars of the infrequent passing parade.

The tools of time

When Ray Gloster was born in 1927, cars were still a rarely seen novelty.

That same year Charles Lindbergh completed the first solo transatlantic flight, the first "talkies" movie was released and federal parliament opened in Canberra.

Ray's father, Arthur "Joe" Gloster, had opened the family garage two years prior, in 1925, and began selling Chevrolet cars the year Ray was born.

"They were selling at 200 pounds each then, imagine that?" Ray says as he sits amid boxes of car parts collected over the decades.

"In 1930, he [Ray's father] swapped buildings with someone that had a store in the front. He always wanted to be on the main street, and the other garage was on the side street. So, they did a swap.

"We sold Chevrolets, Pontiacs, Oldsmobiles and then Holdens until they said they didn't want to deal with us anymore, and they closed down the year after that.

The Glosters have a rich history of business and community involvement in Underbool. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

Ray has fond memories of the first Holden rolling into the workshop in 1948, the FX. He still thinks it was the best model produced and was his favourite car to work on.

While the car market has changed, Ray has declared the family is "not getting into electric ones".

"We're not particularly interested in them," he says.

"And out here in the country, I can't see electric cars taking over because you're too far away from help if you get any problems."

Ray Gloster says he has no intention of retiring, even as he approaches his centenary. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

Outside of his work, Ray and his family have a long history of supporting their community.

He has been a justice of the peace, the projectionist at the local town hall's movies and president of the local hospital board and bowls club.

Ray also remembers when his father declared the town needed electricity.

"In 1932 he said, 'I'm sick of these kerosene lights,' and decided to bring electricity to Underbool," Ray says.

"He brought people from Melbourne to install the poles, and wire the homes and businesses."

(From left) Doug Gloster, Ray Gloster, Robert Gloster, Colleen Gloster (Robert's wife), Frankie Gloster and Cameron Gloster. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

A record awaits

As much as Ray may not like attention, he may be in for a large dose of it: A Guinness World Record as the world's oldest mechanic beckons.

The current record holder is Italian mechanic Fabio Sabbioni, who was born on October 27, 1927.

Mr Sabbioni was aged 97 years and 64 days when his record was verified on December 30, 2024.

However, Ray was born on April 15, 1927.

Four generations of Glosters working side by side in the workshop. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

While Ray is older, according to Guinness World Records, he would "need evidence, including proof of age, proof of employment / paid work, confirmation that he has worked as a mechanic at least once a month within the past year, and photographic / documentary evidence of his work over the years".

Ray's family is currently in the process of gathering the paperwork to prove his case.

Family ties

Few businesses can say they spanned five generations; even fewer can say four of those generations still work side by side.

Brothers Robert and Doug Gloster working at the Underbool workshop. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

Ray's sons Doug Gloster and Robert Gloster work alongside him.

Doug, who, along with Robert, took ownership of the business more than 40 years ago, says it was all he wanted to do.

"And to work with your father, I guess. I think it's just wonderful to be able to do that for so many years," Doug says.

Brothers Doug and Robert Gloster grew up at the workshop. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

Robert's son, Cameron Gloster, says he was born into the business, as was his son, Frankie Gloster, the fourth generation working in the workshop.

Cameron Gloster is unsure if his son, Frankie, will carry on the family business. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

Frankie is in year 12 and works at the garage two days a week as part of his studies.

Cameron says the 17-year-old is unsure if he will carry on the family business.

Frankie Gloster's spent countless hours at the workshop and he recently joined the books officially. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

"It's not a big wage place now with living costs and all that. You can't make a lot of money," Cameron says.

However, even if he does not continue the business, Frankie says he wants to stay in Underbool.

"It's just memories from when I first started coming here as a little kid, and then just kept doing things that I want to do, and work with my father, all my parents, my great-grandfather," Frankie says.

" He's 99, and he's as old as the business, pretty much, and it's pretty special. "

A century worth of history is contained neatly on workshop shelves. (ABC News: Tamara Clark)

Plenty in the tank

Despite his age, Ray says he remains fit, although he does not do as much as he once did.

While still actively involved in the workshop, he says he has no plans to stop, even if on quieter days you'll find him in the shop office playing Sudoku or chatting to passers-by as they fill up with fuel on their way through.

"While I can still walk, I'll still come and, you know, make a nuisance of myself here," Ray says.

"If they don't want me out in the workshop, I'll sit here and do some Sudokus.

"I don't take the work away from the boys, but they often need a bit of help holding something. I go around picking up the tools and filling up different containers, and I do change tyres."

World.title: Police release video of killer Bradley Murdoch filmed days before his death
World.content:
Newly released police body-worn vision shows Bradley John Murdoch repeatedly telling officers he "knows nothing" about the location of victim Peter Falconio's body, as they question the notorious outback killer just days before his death.

Northern Territory Police have released the video ahead of the 25th anniversary of Mr Falconio's disappearance on Tuesday.

The 70-second video is believed to be the first time the public has seen vision of the killer since his imprisonment, and shows an ageing Murdoch after decades in jail.

In 2005, Murdoch was convicted and sentenced to life in jail over the murder of Mr Falconio, a 28-year-old British backpacker, and the assault and attempted kidnapping of his girlfriend, Joanne Lees, near the remote Northern Territory town of Barrow Creek on July 14, 2001.

British couple Joanne Lees and Peter Falconio had been on a road trip through Central Australia when they were ambushed near Barrow Creek in 2001. (Reuters)

Last year, 67-year-old Murdoch died from stage-four cancer in palliative care at Alice Springs Hospital, 22 years into his sentence.

He never revealed the location of Mr Falconio's body, despite repeated pleas from Mr Falconio's family and police over the years, and the introduction of "no body, no parole" laws in the NT in 2016.

In the new footage released by NT Police, filmed three weeks before Murdoch's death, two police officers can be seen questioning the killer in the Alice Springs Correctional Centre.

They had intended to play Murdoch a video statement from Mr Falconio's parents — but he refused to watch it.

In the vision, a female officer can be heard asking Murdoch to think about Mr Falconio as if he were his son Quinton and "somebody knew something about where his body is".

Just nine seconds into the video, Murdoch abruptly cuts her off, angrily saying, "I don't know anything about it".

Bradley John Murdoch was arrested in 2003 by police outside an Adelaide courthouse. (Rob Hutchison: AAP)

As the officer calmly tries to get him to confess, Murdoch continues to talk over her.

"You've been told on that answer, right. Move on, next one," he said.

"Don't beat around the bush because I'm just going to cut you short every time.

"I know nothing. Know nothing. I've said this for 22 years. I know nothing."

Former investigator of Falconio's murder speaks out The lead investigator of the 2001 murder of British backpacker Peter Falconio says she is "not surprised, but disappointed" his convicted killer Bradley John Murdoch never revealed the location of his remains.

The officer attempts to interject before an increasingly frustrated Murdoch punches his left fist towards the ground.

"You keep asking these f***ing questions. I know nothing. You know?" he said.

"I'm not thinking about it. I've thought about it. I've thought about it for 22 f***ing years.

"I've been with these fellas [correctional officers] for 22 years, they've all understood what's going on."

Noticeably raising his voice, Murdoch continues his expletive-laden tirade.

"I've said the same story over and over and over, and now you're here at the last minute because I'm f***ing dying," he said.

"Who gives a f*** about me? Well, some people do.

"I don't have information. This is what I'm trying to say to youse, I don't have this information."

Bradley John Murdoch died in Alice Springs Hospital on July 15, 2025. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

As the female officer tries once more to get Murdoch to cooperate, he again interrupts her.

"No, just get this over and done with for f***'s sake, stop moaning and f***ing around with it," he said.

On the same day the video was filmed last year, police increased the reward for information that could lead authorities to Mr Falconio's body to $500,000.

The following week, police officers desperately tried to get Murdoch to reveal the whereabouts of his victim's remains one last time, according to a coronial inquest into his death held earlier this year.

However, that visit lasted just 30 seconds.

Murdoch died on July 15, 2025, without revealing the location of Mr Falconio's remains.

Investigators appealed to Murdoch until the end

In announcing the increased reward at a press conference in June 2025, NT Police Acting Commander Mark Grieve said investigators had made "numerous approaches" to Murdoch over the years, but the killer had repeatedly stonewalled them.

"Unfortunately, the outcome of those conversations rests with Murdoch," he said.

"On all occasions, he has chosen not to positively engage with police."

Appealing to the public, the acting commander said "there may be someone out there" that Murdoch had confided in who could provide answers.

Was Bradley Murdoch guilty? Court transcripts and experts reveal the evidence Conspiracy theories about the murder of Peter Falconio dogged his family and girlfriend Joanne Lees for as long as Bradley Murdoch denied his guilt. So where does the truth lie?

"Whether or not that's family or friends, we just don't know," he said.

Acting Commander Grieve said police were hopeful the $500,000 reward could help solve the mystery that had "captured worldwide attention", so police could offer "at least some sliver of resolution to Peter's family by bringing home his remains".

"We recognise the passage of time that's transpired, however it's never too late to reach out and at least start that conversation with police," he said at the time.

" You just never know how beneficial that information, that you may hold, may be — essentially, you just don't know what you know. "

Following Murdoch's death, his family released a statement in which they described him as "a devoted father, father-in-law and proud poppy" who "was much more than the headlines".

Mr Falconio's parents, Joan and Luciano Falconio, also released a statement, thanking NT Police for "continuing to investigate our son's murder" even after Murdoch passed away.

"We didn't have much faith, but we were hoping Bradley John Murdoch would reveal where Peter was before he died," they said.

World.title: The World Cup just had one of its hottest matches, in a challenge for the sport
World.content:
As football's greatest sporting rivalries are on show at the World Cup, a common enemy is stalking athletes and players of all stripes in equal measure: heat.

North America is still in the grips of a record-breaking heatwave.

Those tuning into tomorrow morning's World Cup semifinal between Norway and England can expect a rather sweaty affair, with the "feels-like" temperature in Miami expected to hit 43 degrees Celsius.

There is even talk that heat protocols could result in the game being postponed, but that seems unlikely given the television ratings on the line.



Last Sunday, players slogged their way through what is being called one of the hottest games in the tournament's history, when France squared off against Paraguay in Philadelphia amid early evening temperatures hovering around 38C.

France goalkeeper Mike Maignan hydrates ahead of his World Cup match against Paraguay. (AP: Martin Meissner)

It follows searing conditions during the group stage games, nine of which met global players' union FIFPro's thresholds for delay or postponement.

The only two matches thought to be hotter than France vs Paraguay were played in broad daylight over 30 years ago at the first American World Cup, when temperatures on the field reportedly reached 43C and 48C in Florida and Texas respectively.

The pitch and rafters of Philadelphia Stadium were almost certainly hotter than the forecast, with on-field temperatures possibly exceeding 43C.

"Especially for these outdoor stadiums, [you have] a restriction of airflow … so when you're on the pitch, you're not really getting the natural wind … you've got the direct sun beating down on the pitch," said Climate Central meteorologist Shel Winkley.

Body heat radiating from tens of thousands of fans and the stadium itself, composed of concrete and steel, also contributed.

"You're essentially making this little microclimate inside of what is a bigger dome of heat that we experienced over Philadelphia," he said.

Players were not the only ones feeling the heat ahead of Paraguay vs France. (Reuters: Jeenah Moon)

What has led to this exceptional heat? The answer, according to Mr Winkley, is climate change driven by human activities.

"We knew that going into this match, there was an over 60 per cent chance that [the athletes] would experience some sort of performance-impairing heat, which is a temperature of above [28C]," he said.

"We know that with the carbon emissions we've put into the atmosphere, that those percentage points were raised by about 17 per cent.

" That temperature was made at least three to four times more likely because of climate change. "

How hot is too hot?

The heat conundrum is something organisers are keenly aware of and have taken steps to manage better this time around.

Artificial turf has been banished, mandatory three-minute hydration breaks introduced and, to the detriment of millions of European viewers, no matches have been scheduled in Florida before 5pm.

Games in Texas are being played in expensive, climate-controlled stadiums.

Football governing body FIFA's own rules dictate play should be reconsidered when the wet-bulb temperature, a measure that takes the cloistering effects of humidity into account, reaches 32C. The player's union argues it should be lower.

Researchers at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil found the sweet spot for an elite footballer's performance was lower humidity weather, below 22C. The worst was 28C and above.

Hydration breaks have been an unpopular addition among fans who argue they ruin the flow of the game. (Reuters: Amanda Perobelli)

Scientist Matt Brearly, who served as the heat specialist for the Australian Olympic Team at Beijing in 2008, says professional athletes are much better at dealing with temperatures that would send average people to the emergency department, but there are limits.

"We start to see their performance be impaired … if they're playing man on man, they may start to zone off and you see them limiting their physical exertion," he said.

"That's the brain controlling them saying, 'We can't keep producing this much heat, we're overheating.'"

Lewis Miller takes a drink during Australia's clash with Japan. Added drinks breaks will be mandatory at the 2026 World Cup. (Getty Images: James Worsfold)

Telltale signs a footballer might be experiencing heat stress include drooping, slouching and stumbling around the pitch. They will have difficulty communicating with teammates.

"And ultimately, if that isn't enough for them to be substituted and they continue to expose themselves and continue to produce heat, they'll collapse," Dr Brearly said.

The future of World Cup tournaments

Qatar's winning bid to host the 2022 tournament, in a flat barren desert, was widely panned among fans as the ultimate symbol of FIFA's corruption.

How on earth could a football tournament be held in summer in a desert, so the thinking went.

Hydration break farce the ultimate insult for weary World Cup fans Football fans are forced to endure much to keep their love of the beautiful game alive, but FIFA's cynical new "hydration breaks" are stretching the friendship like never before.

The answer, move it to winter, up-ended the schedules of premier leagues the world over.

The deeply unpopular decision is set to be repeated for the 2034 tournament in Saudi Arabia.

But in the future it may have to be repeated for host nations outside of the Gulf.

Conditions are even hotter at this World Cup than in Qatar and those expecting a reprieve at the next one may need to adjust their expectations.

It is due to be co-hosted over the same period in 2030 in Southern Europe, currently dealing with its own record-breaking heatwaves, and Morocco.

Climate-related weather delays can have economic ramifications and negatively affect the fan experience. (AP: Seth Wenig)

These quandaries are not limited to the World Cup. A warmer planet has the potential to change how billions of fans experience their favourite sports.

"If we continue to experience the trends that we're on, can we safely play the games outside, or do we need to start investing in more infrastructure that brings these games inside?" Mr Winkley said.

" Soccer, American football, cricket, baseball, whatever it might be, it really changes what you remember of the game when you were a kid, and maybe how you're experiencing the game with your children. "

Turkish tennis player Zeynep Sonmez helps a ball girl after she collapsed in the heat at the 2026 Australian Open. (Reuters: Edgar Su)

Dr Brearly said hot weather's effect on sport had been gradual.

"I call it climate creep sometimes because the term climate change, people say, 'Well, has it changed?'" he said.

"It hasn't changed, it's creeping along.

"Thirty years ago [spectators in the Northern Territory] could watch a game of football and even the day games weren't too bad in the shade.

World.title: Curbing well-off taxpayers' access to key programs could save billions
World.content:
John Howard once likened the struggle for economic reform to "the runner who is pursuing an ever-receding finishing line".

"If you don't keep running, you don't try to reach it, then others are going to go past you."

Howard used that line in a 2005 speech in Washington. A little over two years later he and the Coalition's 11-year run in office ended in defeat to Kevin Rudd.

In the lead-up to the 2007 election, Labor accused the Howard government of giving up on structural reform. Of losing the appetite for change. Of neglecting infrastructure investment and allowing the economy to drift.

It's been nearly a year since the Albanese government's economic reform summit which was birthed in the wake of Labor's huge 2025 election win.

Expectations were raised that the government would deliver significant changes, that it would attend to problems.

The government claims it has achieved that in the form of ending negative gearing for property and increasing capital gains taxes.

But it would be risky to think the job is now done.

The numbers, like the hips in Shakira's song, don't lie.

Labor, Greens cut deal on CGT and negative gearing The Greens pledge their support in exchange to a delay on the overhaul of the NDIS.

Productivity growth remains firmly stuck in the doldrums. According to the OECD, Australians have experienced one of the sharpest declines in living standards in the developed world since the pandemic.

The International Monetary Fund this week downgraded Australia's economic outlook and now ranks our economy 18th out of 30 advanced countries.

Analysts at Deloitte predicted the economy will limp along over the next two years at a pace that would be the weakest since the early 1990s recession.

"Australia is now structurally exposed in ways that have become hard to ignore," wrote Deloitte Access Economics partner Stephen Smith.

"Deloitte Access has rarely adopted such a downbeat assessment of the short-term outlook."

A rare public rebuke

The bleakness is not confined to the economy. The budget is forecast to remain in deficit for years to come, and in spite of the government's tax increases.

Fixing the shortfalls amid competing political demands for bigger income tax cuts and rising defence, childcare and aged care spending is a paradox in action.

On Friday, the head of the independent Parliamentary Budget Office delivered a rare public rebuke of how governments can deploy otherwise legitimate budgeting rules to flatter the fiscal bottom line.

"Australia has a strong and credible budget framework," Sam Reinhardt said in a speech. "But even strong systems create incentives. And those incentives shape the way policies are developed, presented and debated."

The budget, Reinhardt said, is a bit like a map: "Incredibly useful, but it's not the actual territory. And sometimes the way the map is drawn — or folded — can make some parts of the landscape easier to see than others."

The budget is forecast to remain in deficit for years to come, and in spite of the government's tax increases. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

This includes the use of common budget conventions — some might call them tricks or tactics — such as increased "off-budget" investments, the "contingency reserve" to hide future spending plans, and an excessive focus on new but marginal changes at the expense of the whole picture.

"The common theme is not that any of these features are flaws. Each has a purpose. But if we are not careful, they can narrow the debate — shifting attention away from the merits of policy and towards the way those policies appear in the budget."

Reinhardt doesn't limit her concerns to the federal government alone and warns that rising forecasts for state and territory debt levels will complicate the picture.

"As PBO's soon-to-be-released Medium-Term Budget Outlook publication will show, recent growth in total state gross debt presents a fiscal risk that warrants monitoring, with state debt increasing faster than Commonwealth debt," she said.

"The International Monetary Fund noted in its latest assessment of Australia that, 'as the Commonwealth is viewed as a de facto guarantor of state debt by some credit rating agencies, higher sub-national debt could eventually impact Commonwealth borrowing costs'."

Could means testing come back in fashion?

The speech is a noteworthy and thoughtful intervention in a budget debate that can so often feel repetitive and never-ending.

Howard's runner is not just chasing an impossible finish line. He's running on a circular track.

There are, of course, many levers governments can pull to address budget problems and what is considered sensible or politically prudent changes with time and context.

Budget ideas are also like brown suits. They come in and out of fashion.

One example is the notion of means testing welfare and entitlements. This idea is well and truly out of fashion.

Ever since the global financial crisis and more notably since the pandemic, governments have shunned limits on handouts based around income or wealth.

Political failure to attend to this trend has produced a costly legacy.

A new report — revealed in this week's Insiders on Background podcast — seeks to reprise what in today's context feels like political heresy.

With the economy in the doldrums, Albanese looks to AI for the answer The government can read the numbers, and one thing they tell us is that without refuelling that vital growth agent, productivity, we will stay in the doldrums.

Published by the relatively new Policy Institute Australia thinktank, Home truths: the case for rebalancing toward better means testing, argues that wealthier Australians are receiving billions of dollars a year in taxpayer-funded support.

Curbing access to just four big programs — the child care subsidy, parental leave pay, aged care and pensions — for some of the most well-off taxpayers would free up about $21 billion a year, they calculate.

It is money that could be redirected to those who need it the most.

"We've allowed the wealthiest amongst us to qualify [for] some pretty substantial amounts of benefits," Peter Harris, a former Productivity Commissioner and senior public servant, tells Insiders on Background.

"If we reduce that a bit and reallocate it to the least well off, we'll still be $20 billion in front a year."

Harris, who advised prime minister Bob Hawke on economic reform and was appointed by former Labor treasurer Wayne Swan to the Productivity Commission job, acknowledges that re-introducing means testing would be politically challenging.

"I'm pretty confident that you'd find a unity ticket … between every political party in Australia to say, 'Oh no, we're not going to touch this sort of thing'," he says.

That political reluctance is based on "a fear we are going to have to embrace".

Harris insists that absent changes there’s “nothing in the budget structure” as it stands today that suggests the deficit gap will be bridged in the future.

"We need to start planning now … to think about how we have better means testing and therefore better targeting of our programs so that they go to those most in need."

Loading

What about rethinking the family home?

Among the most risky would be to rethink the treatment of the family home.

The report notes that current rules allowed a retired couple with a $5 million Sydney home to qualify for the full age pension of almost $50,000 a year, while neighbours next door who are renting with $1.5 million superannuation get nothing from the pension.

It also points out that the home owner couple qualifies for up to $150,000 in aged-care support for one spouse, while the renter couple would get around half that sum.

"By means testing, what we mean is if you can contribute more, you should be able to," Harris says.

He says the report has not just focused on older taxpayers' ability to fund their own needs.

"It's not ageist. It is simply about your income or your income and your wealth and how you qualify."

He adds: "Recipients of the age pension and aged care are sensitive groups, we didn't just target old people … we went for paid parental leave and for childcare too."

Taxpayers will shell out about $2.6 billion this year to households with incomes of $300,000+ per year in childcare subsidy and parental leave payments, the report says. (Four Corners)

The report suggests reducing the current "very high" thresholds for the childcare subsidy and parental leave pay from about $500,000 a year in family income to a "substantially lesser amount".

Taxpayers will shell out about $2.6 billion this year to households with incomes of $300,000 per year or more in childcare subsidy and parental leave payments, the report states.

Supporters of the current system say the subsidies are an important driver of workforce participation, particularly among mothers.

But Harris argues that applying means testing is aimed at the top 10 per cent of income earners: a cohort for whom childcare subsidies are not a factor in whether they work or not.

High income earners have a "powerful incentive to go back to work, and the data does show they do", he says.

"In this country we've had two serious goes at applying and then increasing substantially childcare support [and] we've had relatively small improvements … in workforce participation.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

"That's because the natural incentives are there anyway for people to go back to work.

"Where we have had clear benefits, it's been amongst low-income earners and we're saying: increase support for them. Make sure they have even more support but effectively redistribute it from those who really don't need it."

Harris says the report does not nominate an income level at which means testing should apply.

But he does offer his own view.

"My instinct … is it's about $180,000 to $200,000 a year when most people are saying, 'Gee, above that you probably can help yourself more than require the taxpayer to help you'."

There was a time when that wasn't a novel idea.

Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.

World.title: King and Queen meet with Prince Harry, Meghan and children
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family King and Queen meet with Prince Harry, Meghan and children Danica Kirka and Brian Melley Updated July 11, 2026 — 6:01am ,first published 4:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: King Charles III hosted Prince Harry and met with his family for the first time in years on Friday as they try to repair a rift that has persisted since his youngest son and wife quit royal life and moved to America six years ago. Harry, Meghan and their two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, met with the King and Queen Camilla at Highgrove House, a country estate west of London, Buckingham Palace confirmed. King Charles, pictured in Oxford on Friday. Getty Images The Duke of Sussex had arrived on Monday in his homeland for a number of charity events that were overshadowed by speculation of whether he would meet with his father. British tabloids and news broadcasts were filled with speculation about whether Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, would accompany him and, more importantly, whether they would bring their two children so they can finally get to know Grandpa Charles.



However, the monarch’s schedule is often years in the making, with events penciled in long before they take place. An opportunity to hold such a meeting would have been fleeting, particularly because the children would need to return to school in the fall and because they live in California. Prince Harry in Birmingham on Friday at a pickleball event for the Invictus Games. Getty Images The wish to seize the moment fuelled tensions between Harry and royal officials earlier this week. That was highlighted by embarrassing scenes when royal officials first invited Harry to stay at Buckingham Palace, then rescinded the offer after the prince didn’t accept it in a timely manner. Harry’s visit also coincided with him losing his final lawsuit in his quest to tame the British tabloids. A judge ruled that he failed to prove his privacy invasion claims against the publisher of the Daily Mail. His legal battles have been a source of friction with his family, however. Harry has said he wants to reconcile with his 77-year-old father, who is being treated for an undisclosed form of cancer.



Related Article Analysis

Royal family Here’s how it all went wrong in Harry’s ‘creepy’ hacking case. No wonder he’s furious Harry and Charles met briefly for a cup of tea in September during a short visit in London, the first time they’d seen each other in well over a year. But the prince has also wanted his children to see the monarch, whom they first met during celebrations for the late Queen Elizabeth II’s Platinum Jubilee in 2022. The royal children, Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, are now old enough to remember meeting their grandfather, and will certainly hope for pictures with the king, though the event was deemed private and no images will be publicly released. Tensions within the House of Windsor have heightened ever since Harry and Meghan gave up their royal duties and moved to California to pursue lucrative media deals, free from the pressures of royal life in London.



They reached a new low after Harry published an explosive memoir that included unflattering depictions of the royal family and damning allegations of a toxic relationship between the monarchy and the press. Harry’s description of royals leaking information about other family members in exchange for positive coverage of themselves is just one of the tawdry allegations in his book, “Spare.” The prince was especially scathing about Camilla, accusing her of feeding private conversations to the media as she sought to rehabilitate her image after her longtime affair with Charles when he was heir to the throne. Related Article Royal family King takes charge of battle tank after embarrassing mix-up over Harry’s palace lodgings After losing a court battle over his security issue last year, Harry said he hoped to rebuild relations with his family, even as he suggested that the royals had sought to prevent him from receiving police protection to punish him for walking away from royal duties. “I would love reconciliation with my family. There’s no point in continuing to fight anymore,” Harry told the BBC. “I don’t know how much longer my father has.”
